steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Stars form in nebulae: gravity pulls gas and dust together, forming a protostar that heats up until fusion begins

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Main sequence: the longest stable phase where hydrogen fuses to helium in the core; the Sun is currently here

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Low-mass stars (<8 solar masses) expand to red giants, shed outer layers as planetary nebulae, leaving white dwarfs

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: High-mass stars (>8 solar masses) expand to red supergiants, then explode as supernovae, leaving neutron stars or black holes

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Q: Describe the lifecycle of a star like the Sun. | Q: What happens to a star more than 8 times the mass of the Sun? | Q: What is the Chandrasekhar limit?

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: Nebula → protostar → main sequence (hydrogen fusion) → red giant (helium fusion) → planetary nebula → white dwarf. | It becomes a red supergiant, undergoes further fusion stages up to iron, then explodes as a supernova. The core becomes a neutron star (if <3 M☉) or a black hole (if >3 M☉). | ~1.4 solar masses — the maximum mass a white dwarf can have. Above this, electron degeneracy pressure cannot support it and it collapses further.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Draw the lifecycle paths: low-mass vs high-mass — they diverge after the main sequence The Sun has ~5 billion years of main-sequence life remaining A planetary nebula has NOTHING to do with planets — it's a historical name White dwarfs cool over billions of years to become black dwarfs (theoretical — none exist yet)
